summary:
Saudi Arabia has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and the Sunnah, so penalties for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are unpredictable: flogging, fines, lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment, and death in the most severe cases. Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women.

Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence, not merely incidental conduct attached to another charge. No legal gender recognition is available, there is no protection from discrimination, and no relationship recognition. LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Enforcement is documented. In October 2021 five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media. In April 2005, dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and behaving as women at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced in a closed trial without defence lawyers to a total of 14,200 lashes and up to two years' imprisonment.

Foreign nationals face deportation as a penalty for homosexuality, and work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, with infected foreigners deported. Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation but does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status. In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal.

Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground. Amnesty International documented a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for social media posts published before he arrived in the country.

A Pakistani transgender woman, Mohammad Amin, died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh. Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition; Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, and the family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. The most recent documented death in this record is that case; no later instance is documented.

Being transgender is not recognised in Saudi Arabia. UK foreign travel advice states that trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care, and advises couples to avoid public affection. The Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated in May 2023 to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected; homosexuality nonetheless remains illegal and enforcement is described as not universal.

Tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law fining public displays of affection and immodest clothing. In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-colored products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality, explicitly targeting 'the young generation' and confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs.

A3M Global Monitoring's 2024/25 LGBTQ+ Risk Map places Saudi Arabia among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers, in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan. The ranking is by overall placement, not by a per-capita or incident rate.
tangentialFactors:
Public education is required to teach Islamic values strongly condemning homosexuality. Ministry of Education textbooks stated that homosexuality is 'one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes' with capital punishment as the penalty for public homosexual intercourse; in 2020 the Ministry was found to have removed the death-penalty condemnation from textbooks. In 2012 the government asked the CPVPV to help expel students judged to be gay or lesbian based on their mannerisms and fashion taste.

Bars and nightclubs are illegal, and public movie theatres, permitted only since 2018, have LGBTQ themes edited out of films, with customs maintaining a banned list of films and TV shows. Appearing to support homosexuality can result in prosecution for individuals and clubs alike, although observers reported that the MDLBeast Soundstorm music festival in Riyadh included public display of LGBTQI+ culture.

The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS and HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion. HIV prevention education for men who have sex with men is minimal, though a 2024 Saudi AIDS National Program report makes some mention of them; private schools, mainly serving expatriates, have discretion over curriculum on homosexuality.

Human Rights Watch's Scott Long stated of the 2005 Jeddah sentences that prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in Saudi Arabia, so no domestic advocacy machinery exists for residents. There is no legal gender recognition, no discrimination protection, and no relationship recognition for residents.

Residents face the same uncodified sharia penalties as visitors for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, but without the exit option: deportation applies to foreigners, while Saudi nationals face imprisonment, flogging and, in the most severe cases, death.

Residents who are HIV-positive face particular exposure because work-permit renewal requires an HIV test; the designated AIDS/HIV hospitals are the reliable point of care, as other facilities often refuse treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record does not resolve how often the death penalty is actually imposed for same-sex conduct in current practice, as opposed to being available in law; the sources state it as a maximum in the most severe cases without a documented recent execution for this offence.

Whether the May 2023 Saudi Tourism Authority statement and the VisitSaudi welcome messaging reflect any change in enforcement practice is unresolved in these sources; enforcement is described as not universal but no quantified enforcement rate is given.

The 2013 proposal to test and ban gay foreigners was downplayed by officials as a mere proposal; whether any testing regime was implemented is not documented here.

The date of Mohammad Amin's death in custody is not stated in the source inventory, so the recency of that case relative to other incidents cannot be fixed.
